item.title: Getting Started with Laravel and Creating a Project
item.author: kc@example.com (kc kim)
item.description:
Preparing Laravel

Laravel is a PHP Web application framework. It is based on the so-called MVC architecture, which structures applications with Model, View, and Controller, and plays a similar role to frameworks such as CakePHP.

Laravel is available at the following site.

https://laravel.com/

The Korean site is as follows.

https://laravel.kr/

Here, we will not download and install Laravel software directly. Laravel is installed with a package management tool. In this section, we will use the PHP package manager Composer.

Preparing Composer

Composer is available at the following address.

https://getcomposer.org/

Download and install the Composer installer from there. Project creation and related tasks are all performed with Composer, so there is no special need to install Laravel itself separately.

Composer is executed as a command from the command prompt. Start the command prompt and run composer. If the Composer command list appears, Composer is ready to use.

If a message appears saying that composer is not recognized as an internal or external command, executable program, or batch file, the Composer path has not been added. Composer is stored in one of the following locations.

C:\ProgramFies(x86)\ComposerSetup\bin;
C:\ProgramData\ComposerSetup\bin;

composer.bat should be in one of these. Add the path that contains the file to the path variable.

Creating a Laravel Project

Let us create a Laravel example. Laravel development is done by creating a “project.”

A project is a bundle that gathers all files and settings needed for the application you are building. Laravel development basically starts by creating a project, then adding and editing the necessary files in it.

Project creation is done by executing the composer command from the command prompt.

Creating a Laravel Project

composer create-project laravel/laravel project-name --prefer-dist

composer create-project laravel/laravel is a little long, but it is the Composer command that creates a Laravel project. Put the project name after this command. --prefer-dist relates to where packages are downloaded from, and you specify either --prefer-source or --prefer-dist.

Now create a project named myapp. Open the command prompt, move with cd to the location where you want to save the project, and run:

composer create-project laravel/laravel myapp --prefer-dist

This creates a folder named myapp in the current directory and stores the necessary files in it.

About Laravel Installation

Laravel can be used through Composer, but if you want to use it more easily, you can use the Laravel installer. Run the following command from the command prompt.

composer global require "laravel/installer=~1.1"

This installs the Laravel program. Then add the Laravel installer location to the path variable.

C:\Users\user-name\AppData\Roaming\Composer\vendor\bin;

Replace user-name with the appropriate name. This makes the Laravel installer available. With it, you can create a project easily as follows.

laravel new project-name

Run this from the command prompt to create a project. For myapp, simply enter laravel new myapp.

There is no difference in the created project whether you use Composer or the Laravel installer. Use whichever method you prefer.

Running a Laravel Project

Now run the created project.

Work on a Laravel project is performed with a program called artisan. First, move into the project with the cd command.

$ cd myapp

Then start the built-in server. Laravel can start a project as a Web application in the local environment by using its built-in server program.

$ php artisan serve

artisan is a PHP program. After the php artisan command, specify the action to run as an option. Specifying serve starts the built-in server. Once it runs, access the following address from a Web browser.

http://localhost:8000/

A page with Laravel 5 in the center appears. This is the running screen of the created project. The project includes this page as a sample by default.

To stop the program, select the command prompt where it is running and press Ctrl + C. The server program stops and returns to the input waiting state.

Laravel Project Structure

Open the created project folder and look inside. You will see many folders. Here is a brief explanation.

  • app folder: The main body of the application. PHP programs for application development are placed here.
  • bootstrap folder: The bootstrap program for the application. It contains startup and preparation processing.
  • config folder: Contains various application configuration files.
  • database folder: Contains files related to databases.
  • public folder: The public folder. Ordinary HTML files that do not use MVC architecture are placed here.
  • resources folder: Contains resource files used by the application. MVC view template files are placed here.
  • storage folder: A folder for data storage. Session, cache, and similar files are created here.
  • tests folder: Contains files related to unit tests.
  • vendor folder: Contains programs and libraries created by vendors.

There are many other files, but they are omitted because there is nothing special we need to work on for now. Of the many folders, the important ones are app, config, public, and resources.

Use app whenever you do actual programming. Use config, for example, when configuring the database. Use public when installing ordinary HTML files. Use resources when installing templates for screen display.

The others are not used immediately, so you do not need to memorize them yet. For now, roughly remember the role of these four folders.

app Folder

Among the folders in the project, the most important is the app folder. This is where the main parts of the Laravel application are placed.

The app folder contains several folders.

  • Console folder: Contains console programs, or command programs.
  • Events folder: Contains event programs.
  • Exceptions folder: Contains programs related to exception handling.
  • Http folder: Contains processing related to HTTP access. The basic programs you create for the application are included here.
  • Jobs folder: Contains programs, or jobs, that are added to queues and executed.
  • Listeners folder: Contains event listener programs.
  • Policies folder: Contains authentication processing programs called policies.
  • Providers folder: Contains programs called service providers.

There may be many items here that are unfamiliar, but many are not used for a while, so you do not need to memorize all of them. The one you must remember is the Http folder. When you start programming in Laravel, you will first install a program called a controller in this Http folder. Remember this Http folder.

Http Folder

Inside the important Http folder are more folders and files.

  • Controllers folder: Contains programs called controllers.
  • Middleware folder: Contains middleware, programs that act like filters.
  • Requests folder: Contains request-related programs.
  • Kernel.php: Contains the HTTP kernel, which becomes the HTTP access middleware.
  • routes.php: Contains routing programs that assign processing to accessed addresses.

For now, remember Controllers and routes.php, because you will use them immediately when actual programming begins.

This completes the overview of the project structure. Next, we will start actual programming.

item.title: Laravel Routing and Controllers
item.author: kc@example.com (kc kim)
item.description:
Routing and routes.php

When developing a Web application, the first thing to think about is routing. Routing means assigning what processing should be performed when a certain address is accessed.

When no framework was used, Web development was simple. If you placed a file named helo.php in a folder named myapp under the public folder, accessing /myapp/helo.php called that file.

Frameworks do not use that simple approach. The whole application is controlled by the framework, and required programs are called and executed when needed. The framework manages which program should run and which file should be displayed when a certain address is accessed. This is routing.

In Laravel, routing is performed by the routes.php file in the Http folder under app. If you open this file, you will see script code. The important calls can be summarized as follows.

Route::get(XX);
Route::group(XX);

Routing is configured by calling static methods provided by the Route class. These methods take two arguments.

Route::method(value, function);

The first argument represents information such as the address assigned to the route. Its content differs depending on the method. For get, it is text representing an address, while group may use an array that groups address information. The second argument is the processing called when that address is accessed. The value returned by this function becomes the result of accessing the address. You can return text directly, return a template file such as HTML, or specify processing that calls a controller.

Methods of the Route Class

The main methods for routing settings are as follows.

Route::get(address, function);

Sets routing for GET access. The first argument is the assigned address as text. If the second argument function returns text, that text is output directly.

Route::post(address, function);

Sets routing for POST access. Basic usage is the same as get.

Route::put(address, function);
Route::delete(address, function);

HTTP also has PUT and DELETE access methods. These are used for modification and deletion.

Route::any(address, function);
Route::match(array, address, function);

These support multiple HTTP methods. any routes all HTTP methods, such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE. match prepares an array of HTTP method names as the first argument, for example ['get', 'post'], and routes access for those methods.

Let us make a simple example. Add the following code to routes.php.

Route::get('/helo', function () {
    return '<html><body><h1>Hello World</h1><p>this is sample page.</p></body></html>';
});

Start the server and visit the following address.

http://localhost:8000/helo

When accessed, a page titled Hello World is displayed. This display is generated by the Route::get method.

In the example, the first argument of the get method is /helo. When this address is accessed, the HTML text returned by the second argument function is sent back and displayed as is. In this way, routing alone can display something on the screen for a given address.

Creating a Template

Returning HTML code as text from a Route class method makes it difficult to create complex displays. It is easier to prepare an HTML file in advance, load it, and use it.

Laravel lets you prepare templates for screen display and use them to display pages. These templates are placed in the views folder inside the application’s resources folder.

Create a simple template. In the views folder, create a PHP file named helo.php and write the following source code.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>Sample</title>
    <style>
    body { color:gray; }
    h1 { font-size:18pt; font-weight:bold; }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <h1>Sample</h1>
    <p><?php echo $message; ?></p>
</body>

As you can see, this is very simple HTML code. However, one PHP tag is included in the middle.

<p><?php echo $message; ?></p>

This outputs the value of the variable $message. A template is prepared as a very ordinary PHP file like this. There is nothing special about it.
